CHAPTER XLVIII.
The ornamental tree (Kalpavriksha-vidhana).

The name of the chapter is Kalpavriksha, which literally
means a mythical tree granting all wishes or, in other words,
an all-productive tree. But here it is undoubtedly a decorative
device surmounting a seat (@san) or throne. It is also found in
connection with the muktaprapinga, the mandapa, and the ma-
karatorana.
The minute description and measurement of all the various
parts of the tree are given. Its trunk (pada) is wound with a
serpent, with expanded five-fold hood. The measurements of tho
snake, of its hood, and of its tail are described in detail. The
number of branches as well as their size varies according to the
special purpose of the throne, for the decoration of which the

CHAPTER L.

In the first verse it is announced that the chapter is devoted

reality only the first part of the chapter deals with ornaments
proper, whereas the remaining portion deals with certain mis-
cellaneous articles, such as lamp-posts, fans, mirrors, swings,

same category.
The Manasara calls the former ‘ornaments of the body’ (anga-

Ornaments proper are here divided into four classes, namely, —
patra-kalpa, chitra-kalya, ratna-kalpa, and migrila. All these are
suited to the deitics. The emperor or universal monarch (chak-

CHAPTER LI.
The triad (Trimiurti-lakshana-vidhana) ').

The Indian Triad, to which the title of the chapter refers, con
sists of the three great gods Brahma, Vishnu and Siva. The

‘chapter may be divided into two parts. The first part deals with

the materials (dravya) of which the idols of these three deities
as well as all other images are made. The second part describes
the external features of the Triad.
The materials for making idols are nine, namely, gold, silver,
copper (témra), stone, wood, sudhka@ (stucco; also mortar and
plaster), sarkar@ (lit. gravel or grit), @bhaisa (marble?) and earth
(terra-cotta), All the materials enumerated are well known except
abhasa, of which a special description is given.
Abhisa is subdivided into three kinds, called chitra, ardha-
chitra, and abhasa proper. If it is perpectly transparent (sarvaiga-
drisyamaina, lit., which can completely be seen through) it is
called chitra; if only half transparent, it is known as ardha-
chitra; and in case it is partially (lt. one fourth) transparent, it
is called @bhisa proper. This description, however, does not help
us to identify a@bkdsa with any certainty. It may have some
affinity to crystal, but the latter has been referred to elsewhere
by its own common name, sphatika. The ordinary meaning of
the word a@bhisa is splendour, light, transparency. It implies un-
doubtedly a transparent substance. I am inclined to think that
it may refer to some particular and more or less transparent
variety of marble (alabaster?) of which various other kinds, such
as white, black, red, yellow, etc., are described in the next
chapter in connection with the materials of which the pitha or
yoni part of the phallus (Higa) of Siva is made.
The second part begins with the different classes of images.
An idol may be stationary (sth@vara) or movable (jangama) ;
erect, sitting or recumbent. The movable images are used espe-
cially on the occasion of festivals. The three or four poses (bhanga),

CHAPTER ¥.

Jaina images (Jaina-lakshana-vidhana).

The opening: lines describe in detail the various kinds of
measurements used in Indian sculpture.
The lincar measurement is divided into six kinds mana, pramana,
parimana, lambamaina, unmana, and upamana.
The measurement from the foot to the top of the head is
called ména'), which is in fact nothing but height. Pramana is
the measurement of breadth (vistrita); parimina is the measure-
ment of girth or circumference (paritah); ltambamina is the
measurement along the plumb-line, the line drawn perpendicu-
larly through the different parts of the body, the mana or the
measurement of the height being determined by the surface of
the body; wnmdana is the measurement of thickness (ntmna) or
diameter; and upamana is the measurement of interspace (antara),
such as that between the two feet of an image; this measurement
is evidently taken from one plumb-line to another.
The primary measurement (adimna) refers to comparative
measurement and is divided into nine kinds. The height of an
image is determined: 1st, by comparing it with the breadth (ara)
of the whole temple (harmya); 2nd, with the height of the cella
or sanctum (garbhagriha); 3rd, with the height of the door (dvéra-
mina); 4th, with the measurement of the base (adhishthina) ;
5th, by expressing it in hastas; 6th, in the tila system; 7th, in
angulas; 8th, by comparing it with the height of the worshipper ;
and 9th, with the height of the vehicle (va@hana) or with the height
of the principal idol (milabera).
Absolute measurement in cubits (hasta), etc., is given in the

‘case of many architectural and sculptural objects.

The aigula (lit. finger) measurement has reference to both
comparative and absolute measurements. Three kinds of aigulas
are expressly distinguished, and a fourth angula is added later.
a) The berangula is the measurement taken by the afgula or
finger of the main idol; :
